Why are we still having this conversation?

It was clear to every sane person in this country that the combination of Fox analyst witch doctors and Charlie Kirk-inspired hacks assembled by this Administration that fantasy was not going to jibe well with real life.

Now we're sinking fast, and so many of us I used to respect are still wringing their hands wondering how such a catastrophe could befall such a wonderful bunch of people.

Here's my theory: Trump is America. He represents, from his bragging about cheating on his taxes to how he greets beautiful women to his rising from the ashes of every debacle he perpetrates, the American ideal: Power and money without talent or service.

I rewatched The Empire Strikes Back a few years ago, and before long I was laughing uncontrollably. I realized that Americans identified with Luke and Lea, not with Darth Vader. During my lifetime, since 1950, America has not been friendly with even one rag-tag band of misfits trying to bring down someone like, say, Franco or Duvalier or the Shah of Iran. America has been the Empire, or at least its enforcer.

Even today, as we say nice things about Mandela and Dr. King, how many of us are working assiduously to beam back to a day when white people told black people what to do and where to live? There's plenty of a/c in the hotels and in select Airbnbs and short-term rentals, but it's wise to search online with that criteria clearly stated. When in Spain, do as the Spanish do. Get out early. Hug the shady side of the street. Head inside for the main midday meal by 2pm. Follow up with a siesta. Head out again after 8pm, when the night is a bit cooler, the sun is closer to setting (around 9:30), and the night is young. If you head for the main tourist attractions in the middle of the day, you'll be one of those people warning others against European travel in the summer.

This column, and many commenters, operate on a piece of false binary thinking that places an enormous chasm (or ocean) between Amerindian and European concepts of land holding. 

It may come as news to people that stewardship and tenancy-in-common concepts of landholding were far from alien to European understandings. It is true that, with the dawn of the Modern Age the middle of the Second Millennium CE that English concepts of land holding became dominated by what we today call fee simple, but relatively few people held land by fee simple before the Modern Era and even into it. (That's one of the realities that drove people to leave for the New World.) Before that, it was no uncommon to have "common" land - like the richest river flood plain land (which was always vulnerable to being flooded in overly rainy year) whose specific use (or being set aside to remain fallow) in a given growing season would be allocated among freemen, and rotated from year to year. A number of English who settled New England hailed from places that had living memory of that previously longstanding practice.

comments.name: Craig E. Carroll, PhD

The most important distinction in this essay is not between words and action, as though words themselves have no value. It is between words that close an account and words that open one.

A land acknowledgment becomes self-protective when the institution treats the statement as evidence that the matter has been handled. A credible acknowledgment should instead create questions the institution remains responsible for answering: Which living nation are we speaking about? What relationship do we have with it? What changed because we made this acknowledgment? Who owns the commitment, and how will anyone know whether it was fulfilled?

That does not require every institution to promise the same remedy, nor does it reduce the issue to returning every parcel of land. It does require the institution to connect its language to some consequence involving access, resources, stewardship, authority, education or continuing relationship.

The failure is not that acknowledgment is symbolic. Institutional language is always symbolic. The failure comes when the symbol is used as a substitute for responsibility.

An acknowledgment should be the beginning of accountability, not the conclusion of it.

comments.body:
Excellent piece. My wife and I included a land acknowledgment in our wedding ceremony, which was held at a state park where one of those insidious treaties were signed to kick out the Muscogee Creek nations.

We chose to include it not to absolve ourselves or win brownie points. We did it to raise awareness amongst our families about the history of the place so that they would be forced to confront it for themselves.

And it did! My ultra-conservative uncle heard the land acknowledgment and thought it was incredible history. He and others who attended our wedding mentioned it as a highlight. It’s not near enough to force the reckoning we need with our history, but it’s a start.

I also donated part of the gifts we received in our wedding fund to organizations that support the Land Back movement and Indigenous people across our state. I support returning the land to its original stewards, whatever form that takes. National and state parks would be a good start. But eventually, our history of colonization requires a grander reckoning.

AI is ushering in a completely new era of reuse and repurpose. Artists have always had influences that show up in their work - whether it’s from another person or from something they’ve seen or experienced.

Some of it is so bad, no wonder artists aren't concerned. Some others though, compete directly with the remixes made by the artists or their studios themselves. The automation of AI, as with so many other of its other "uses", has now put this "hobby" as well into the reach of those with little or no music ability or particular talent. comments.name: academic
comments.body:
I'm a copyright law professor. Composers make money by licensing the copyright to their compositions. Music (or art or text) generated by AI is not copyrightable without significant human authored expression ( and no, the Copright Office has pointed out, a prompt is not the same thing as human expression).

And if it's not copyrightable, it can't be licensed because it's free for anybody to use. Which eliminates licensing as a source of revenue, leaving only ad revenue from online engagement, which is far less money.

All of that means even if we put aside the aesthetic, an artistic issues of Gen-AI, it's a bad deal for anyone depending upon royalties and licensing... such as the entire music, TV, and film industries.

But none of that information is contained in this article that seems designed to kiss up to tech bros by failing to address the real issues the creative industries are concerned about.

Suddenly bean-counters and lazy wannabes can become “creators” themselves – “Look at me, I can write songs too! Create movies! Write books!” But of course AI never falls in love, never experiences loss or victory. It does not grow so much as it gains mass. It is worse than soulless in that it steals from those with souls and allows others to sell or to violate their sufferings and their triumphs, repackaged and rearranged by committee or by hobbyists. AI for medical issues, engineering, product safety and all of the other technical bits that make the world better, safer and more stable. But to replace the human-ness of being human? To commodify and genericize the human experience into a sort of smoothie bar – “What would you like in your human experience today — a little bit of Bjork’s blood mixed with some tears from Maria Callas over a bangin' beat? Order up!” The arts industry survives, but the actual artists are back to waiting tables. I hate all of this.

comments.name: John

Nuclear power plants are just ridiculously expensive.  

A natural gas power plant costs less than one-tenth and takes a small fraction of time to build compared to nuclear.  Further, nuclear requires a staff of around 1000 to operate and maintain, while a natural gas plant requires 50.  And the nuclear requires much more expensive ongoing investment related to equipment, re-fueling, and spent fuel management during its life cycle.  So until there are disruptive breakthroughs on costs (tried many times without success), nuclear is to remain a minor baseload power source.  

There’s a reason why China has 1100 coal fired power plants in operation and continues to build hundreds more each year, vs. 62 nuclear plants in operation and a few dozen in construction.  (Unfortunately for China and world climate, they do not have significant natural gas reserves, so they are left primarily with coal by default for baseload power.  By the way, the US generates more power from solar than from coal.  Solar surpassed coal in May 2026.  China generates over 55% of their power from coal vs. 11% from solar.)

Renewables are great, but capacity increases are incremental and baseload power is needed to fill in gaps in the highly variable output.  That’s where natural gas comes in in the US and coal in China.  

Of course we should pursue more batteries to compliment renewables.  Everyone likes batteries, except unfortunately when it comes to mining the raw materials.

That would eliminate human freedom, our most treasured "possession." Christians who see God's hand in our affairs neglect this aspect of the Christian God, that our freedom is always safeguarded. Meister Eckhart prayed God to deliver him from all false notions of god, such as that God controls us all. Killer Whales. That's what they are and well deserved. No greater top marine predator.

Orca? Latin. Translated into Death Whale. Feel better about attempting to cutify a such a deadly mammal? The genus name Orcinus means "of the kingdom of the dead", or "belonging to Orcus". Ancient Romans originally used orca (pl. orcae) for these animals, possibly borrowing Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (óryx), which referred (among other things) to a whale species.

A further misnomer is that these are dolphins and therefore not whales. Incorrect, as all species within infraorder Cetacean are whales. Cetaceans are divided into two parvorders - Mysticeti (baleen whales) and Odontoceti (toothed whales). Within that latter order of whales, 6 species within Dolphinoidea (dolphins) have 'whale,' including killer whales, within their common names.

The drones will only do so much, and he knows that if the Russians really want, they can turn Kiev into another Gaza overnight. But right now Russia doesn't seem to have the stomach to do that in Ukraine.

The political turmoil in Kyiv with street protests, a new prime minister, a new defence minister and a new chief of the general staff all within days has shattered the narrative, amplified in much of the media's mainstream coverage, that Ukraine has turned the corner while Russia is supposedly on the back foot. Two weeks ago Zelensky said he would force Russia to the bargaining table in 40 days. Reality is the only thing that brings a measure of sanity to the "Ukraine is winning" narrative.

The rift between outgoing Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and General Syrskyi also seems to reflect a deeper strategic debate: one camp places great faith in high-profile drone strikes deep inside Russia, despite their limited effect in easing pressure on Ukrainian troops defending a 1,200-kilometre front, while the other argues that scarce resources (troops, artillery shells, Patriot air defence missiles, etc.) should instead give priority to exhausted forces amid Russian advances in several fortress cities.

If Ukraine's political and military leadership continues to feud publicly, with Fedorov seemingly reluctant to leave the entire spotlight to Zelensky, Russia will exploit those fractures and intensify pressure on the battlefield. Another Russian mobilization might be in the cards.

Did he respond to the public demonstrations? Yes. Does Fedorov deserve substantial credit for Ukraine’s rise as a drone power? Certainly—but not all of it.

The deeper problem is that the article rearranges and compresses the sequence of events in a way that diminishes Zelensky’s leadership. It judges particular decisions without giving proper weight to what came before: his refusal to run, his persistence when American support was withdrawn, his willingness to respond to public pressure, and the broader wartime leadership under which Ukraine’s drone capabilities developed.

What strikes me about this article is how each culture and each generation has adapted a universally relevant human story to speak to their own time. 

Homer based his epics on stories of a bygone age.  While some of the details of life in the Mycenean period, which is when, Odysseus, if he was based on a real man, would have lived, are surprisingly accurate, he probably changed things around a little to make the story relevant to his much audience the way that medieval poets dressed King Arthur, another man who may or may not have lived, in plate armor.

Greeks saw Odysseus as one of their own: supersmart, brave and capable.  The Romans too saw him as a typical Greek too, smart yes, but a little too slippery to be trusted.

In "Ulysses", the 1950s movie starring Kirk Douglas, he's a fairly uncomplicated hero battling gods and monsters to get home from a war0--a story which resonated with the generation which had won World War II.

Fast forward to the mid 2020s and decades of "forever wars".   

In "The Odyssey" and "The Return" starring Ralph Fiennes, Odysseus is portrayed as a warrior wracked with guilt for what he did in a long war launched by arrogant and foolish leaders. 

There are elements of this in Homer, but previous generations chose to downplay this aspect of the story.   It speaks to our own times however, or at least to some of us.  The online right hates this take on the hero but absolutely loves the earlier "Ulysses".  

That too speaks to our times too.

comments.name: George S.

What this article misstates what is meant by "affordable housing".

The true measure is whether there is adequate housing available in a given region that costs no more than about 1/3 the median income.

I live in Manhattan and, yes, I meet the criteria in this article.

But Manhattan is not a separate region or jurisdiction.  It is a part of NYC that is, itself, a part of a larger metropolitan region.

Moreover, this article simply measure housing cost on the basis of home ownership.

But NYC, including Manhattan, remains a city with a large number of residents living in rental housing.

On that basis, the amount of income needed to rent an apartment in Manhattan is now far greater than this "ownership-based" analysis shows.

For Manhattan, and the greater NY region to thrive it needs to provide rental housing that is, indeed, "affordable".

The most important mechanism used to attempt to achieve that is to provide incentives for developers to build residences with mixed-income components.

In return for various zoning and tax incentives developers set aside a certain proportion of total units that are affordable to primarily middle-income NY'ers.

These units are rentals that may be a portion of a total rental project where the bulk of the apartments are "market".  Or they may be a rental component of a building where the other units are market-rate condos.

The challenge is to build affordable rental housing.

This analysis fails to understand that.
